newsitem.title: USA: Hartford 's life IPO likely winner - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hartford 's life IPO likely winner - analysts.

text.p: Insurance giant The Hartford's decision to spin off up to 20 percent of its life operation as a publically traded company is a long-overdue recognition of the company's "crown jewel," analysts said on Monday.
They said the initial public offering (IPO) will likely be a hit with investors because The Hartford's life business has been growing well above the industry average.
This is thanks in large part to Hartford Life's huge variable annuities business, said analysts, who had been speculating for months that a spinoff was in the works.
"The market is certainly ripe for it," wrote Peter Wade of Lehman Brothers in a published report.

"Life is the crown jewel of The Hartford's operations," said Wade. "It's the annuity business that makes it attractive. They added $12 billion in variable annuities which are low-risk, low-margin, but high ROE businesses, which are high-growth. It's sort of like mutual funds, with a tax-deferred wrapper."

An annuity is a contract that provides a periodic income at regular intervals for a certain time. It is often used to fund retirement. With variable annuities, the amount may fluctuate in relation to securities market values or other factors.
The Hartford's total life revenues grew by 17 percent in 1996 to $4.4 billion. Life core earnings were up by 14 percent to $251 million.
Its individual annuity revenues for 1996 were $616 million, compared with $365 million in 1995.
"Hartford Life has been one of the most rapidly growing life insurance companies in the industry," said Mike Albanese, vice president at A.M. Best Co.

"They've been very innovative in terms of products. They've more or less pioneered, or become the largest writer, of market-value annuities that essentially provide some longer-term protection to the company from disintermediation that might normally be associated with single-premium deferred annuities," said Albanese.
"They're also a major writer of variable annuity contracts, with a wide variety of fund options. Certainly in the bull market, that's been very, very attractive.

"They've also got substantial distribution relationships. Not many companies in the industry have such extensive distribution relationships and have achieved the level of success in terms of sales results."
Analysts said The Hartford could raise up to $800 million through the IPO.
"They're raising capital in the lowest-cost means available and they are also highlighting how undervalued their subsidiaries are," said Wade.

"They have a company embedded within them that has a 15-plus percentage growth rate and probably almost a 20 percent return on equity, that prior to the announcement of this deal was trading at a discount to most property-casualty companies."
Wade said the Hartford Life stock could trade at about 14 times earnings, or about $40 a share.
"This implies that the property-casualty stock is worth $38," he said.
The Hartford's shares were up three to 78-1/4 on 664,200 shares traded at 1530 EST on Monday.
The life spinoff was "the type of option that makes a lot of sense to exercise for The Hartford," said Jack Reichman, associate director at Standard & Poor's.

"They expect to need more capital, which means they expect to keep up the pace of growth that they've had. Instead of downstreaming the funds from the parent, they can raise it directly from the capital markets."
